extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and journalism students (especially cub reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing newspaper news stories (leads, bodies, paragraphs, sentences) with emphasis on accuracy, clarity, tone, and adherence to newsroom policies. Primarily aimed at reporters learning practical news-writing craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead: summary vs informal
rubrics_metrics.description: Two types of lead: the definite summary lead and the informal (suspense/climax) lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginners are advised to attempt only the summary lead at first because it is definite and the reporter can know when it answers who, what, when, where, why, and how. The informal lead seeks a particular effect (climax/suspense) that is elusive; novices should confine themselves initially to summarizing leads and only later attempt informal leads as their hand becomes sure. Examples illustrate how a lead can promise a tone (pathos, humor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match lead to story tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead should suggest the tone of the story (pathetic, tragic, humorous, mildly satirical, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imbuing the lead with the intended story-tone increases the story's success; sample leads demonstrate tonal promise (e.g., tragic vs half-serious humor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Body: maintain interest and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: In the body of the story the reporter's care must be to maintain the interest developed in the lead and to ensure accuracy of succeeding statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically the body is a chronological narration with interspersed explanation/description; good organization of details makes the body nearly write itself. Avoid the two crimes of inaccuracy and dullness; inaccuracy is the greater fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy (strict adherence to truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not draw on imagination or jump to conclusions; present facts accurately with proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inaccurate reporting humiliates the paper later, causes loss of public confidence, and harms innocent people. Provide ample proof for statements in case they are questioned; prefer understatement so future larger figures will be believed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and respect the law of libel
rubrics_metrics.description: Every newspaper person should know the law of libel: what constitutes libel and who is legally responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Libel includes any published matter that tends to disgrace, degrade, or subject a person to public distrust, ridicule, or contempt, including ironic or sarcastic terms. Responsibility may reach owners, publisher, editor, writer, and sellers if awareness can be proved. Lack of intent is not a defense; if injury is proved, damages follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of libel (attribution and limiting phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: When making potentially unpleasant statements about a person, give the name of the source or use limiting phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use phrases like 'it is alleged,' 'it is rumored,' and attribute charges to named authorities. Such phrases do not remove responsibility but lessen it and make later corrections easier; wherever possible give the reporter's authority for claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exaggeration; prefer understatement
rubrics_metrics.description: Extravagant statements defeat their own end and erode reader confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you must err in valuation of news, err toward understatement. Consistent understatement builds reader trust so that when large figures or claims are necessary they will be believed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid editorializing in news columns
rubrics_metrics.description: Present news from an unbiased, colorless standpoint; do not attempt to influence public opinion in news columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal views should not color news articles; that function belongs to editorial columns. Examples show how political or personal bias makes a story unprintable or ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe a paper's editorial policies (follow commands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must learn and observe their newspaper's policies and follow the instructions of managing or city editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern newspapers are business organizations with owners' policies; reporters may be required to feature or frame stories in line with those policies. While ideal is unbiased news, in practice reporters may be expected to write sympathetically or severely as editors request; failure to do so may jeopardize employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of policy among reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper's credibility depends on consistent presentation of policy across its reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reporters present events from widely divergent, distorted angles the paper cannot hold readers' respect or patronage; consistency in tone/policy is important for institutional standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness of the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearness is second only to accuracy: every paragraph must be clear and its relation to others evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep connected ideas together and separate unrelated ideas; maintain consistent verb tenses; for follow-ups include sufficient summary of preceding events; use logical arrangement and grouping to aid clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence (methods to achieve it)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain coherence by arranging facts in natural sequence, using pronouns, repetition, and relation words/phrases/clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical arrangement is the first step; reporters commonly use pronouns and skillful repetition to hold ideas in sequence. Use repetition and pronouns judiciously to maintain flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use relation words sparingly in news writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation words that connect sentences (moreover, finally, on the other hand, etc.) are used sparingly in news writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and readers demand ideas to follow closely with compressed style, reducing need for many connectives; this contributes to the tight 'bing-bing-bing' narrative style but should be balanced with clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse of 'bing-bing-bing' (choppy short-sentence) style
rubrics_metrics.description: The rapid, compressed short-sentence style can be useful in excitement but overused produces fitful, choppy effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence length and include more complex sentences; reserve the very short-sentence barrage for moments of high excitement and not as the default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis through tone and condensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis is achieved by avoiding vague literary phrasing, respecting story tone, and condensing expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone and precision produce emphasis; avoid affectation of literary phraseology which often destroys tone; condense ideas into smallest space consistent with clarity and force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague literary phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not adopt sonorous, grandiloquent phrases that mean little or are vague in the reporter's context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such phrases often are borrowed and lose meaning; they lack the sharp precision needed for news and usually produce a revulsive rather than interesting effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain appropriate and consistent tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone must fit the subject (dignified for weddings, restrained for tragedies) and avoid unintended humorous or unrelated implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful that unrelated ideas don't create unfortunate suggestions; ensure wording and incident placement don't unintentionally alter the intended tone of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied sentence length; aim for medium sentences (~20 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid sentences that are unnecessarily long (heavy) or markedly short (monotonous/choppy); a happy medium is desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twenty words is offered as a good average sentence length. Remember readers include the uneducated; make style fluent and accessible so a reader with a small spoken vocabulary can understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Condense ideas into the smallest space possible; avoid diffuse style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters must follow space limits typically set by city editors; if allotted more space, introduce additional factual details instead of mere words. Efficiency and tightness of expression are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final test of a story: effect upon the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate test of a story's goodness is its effect on the reader: attaining desired result matters more than conformity to models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get accuracy and interest by any effective method; a story that achieves its effect may become a new pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph as a mark of punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: The paragraph sets off larger divisions of the story and functions like punctuation: its indention notifies the reader of a shift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph purpose is clearness and emphasis; treat paragraphing as you would punctuation to aid reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph clearness and relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraphs must be clear and their relation to preceding and following paragraphs evident at a glance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transitional phrases when necessary, but rely mainly on natural and close sequence of ideas for clarity between paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph emphasis: put important details first
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning of each paragraph should contain the most important details to catch a rapid reader's eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid opening paragraphs with dependent clauses or identical constructions; vary openings to maintain reader interest. Paragraphs may be rounded at the end but begin with emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph length: brief and brief-looking
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraphs should be short, and visually brief; long paragraphs repel modern readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-sentence paragraphs are common, especially in leads. Avoid half-column paragraphs; roughly 140 words (20 lines) is the limit, with 8–10 lines a good average. Put each subtopic into its own paragraph; when in doubt, make a new paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence requisites: accuracy, interest, grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences must obey the same laws of accuracy and interest as the story; good grammar is essential because sentences are readily analyzable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even under time pressure, reporters must produce sentences that do not reveal how rushed they were. Faulty, ungrammatical, or weak sentences will lose readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar: avoid faulty reference, incorrect verb forms, poor coordination, and ellipsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Good grammar is the first requirement for accuracy in the sentence; main violations fall into four heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors correct grammatical errors constantly; strive for correct verb forms, proper coordination/subordination, clear references, and acceptable ellipsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronouns referring to ideas (clear reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure every pronoun refers to a particular word in the sentence and agrees in gender and number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using pronouns to refer to general ideas not expressed in a particular word causes ambiguity and ludicrous turns. Verify each pronoun's antecedent to preserve clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement of pronouns in number
rubrics_metrics.description: Make reference words agree in number with the noun they refer to; take care after collective nouns, distributives, or mixed noun lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faulty agreement (e.g., treating 'mob' as plural) pollutes clarity. Watch pronoun-number agreement after words like everyone, anybody, each one, or after combinations of singular/plural nouns.
